en: Had God struck the prince senseless?
To set the bird upon the swan,
And have it bring the swan down,
The poor prince grew eager,
And appealed to the Almighty.
He gripped the falcon on his arm
And drew it close against his side;
He touched Buurul beneath him
With his heel beneath the foreleg.
The young prince made Buurul
Step forward with long, rolling strides,
And trot with a rocking gait;
He sat holding the bird at an angle,
Bringing it into the proper position,
And made the falcon quiver,
Ready to remove its hood.
The tiger who loomed like a mountain
Prepared to cast it headlong,
And made the falcon ready.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
These two legacies left by bygone lions,
Came racing up together,
With Kulchoro crying urgently;
The two of them arrived.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Kulchoro, son of Almambet,
Both a strongman and a lion,
Began speaking these words
To his elder kinsman:
“Kulchoro and Kanchoro—
We two were twin boys,
And souls who became companions to you.
If we choro died,
We were sons worth no more than dog hide;
While we remained alive,
We were servants worth no more than sheepskin.
Having girded his waist firmly,
The brave Semetey
Was born together
With our own selves.
Your dear mother Kanykey,
Who shared the bloodline of Manas, now gone beyond,
Came forth wounded from her womb;
Look here, tiger—
When were we ever sons of Manas?
My poor elder kinsman, hear my words.
Though we are servants, if we grow unruly,
While you, my khan and elder, are here,
And rage and swallow our anger,
If we set the bird upon the swan
And drink our fill of joy,
While our tiger elder is present,
Let us cough loudly together
And raise our downcast spirits!
When you mounted a horse, you mounted indeed,
My elder, Prince Semetey—
What horns have you suddenly grown?
Your Akshunkar should alight
Upon the hands of these two;
If you fly the falcon alone,
You would need two heads!”
While the boys spoke in this way,
The world lay level around them,
And the sea spread out like this;
When one looked into its depths,
It seemed broader than the face of the earth.
He could not say of the falcon on his hand,
“I will not give it,”
Nor turn away the brave man’s wish;
The famous heir of Manas
Handed over the falcon.
Eager to fly it at the swan,
Kulchoro took it,
Steadied all his thoughts,
And settled the white falcon on his hand.
Taking the falcon, Kulchoro
Fastened and secured it again,
Attached Akshunkar’s long leash
To the belt around his waist,
Hurried Semetey onward,
Though he did not know the proper way to the contest,
Not knowing the manner of how
One should approach the swan,
He came trotting with pounding hooves,
Saying, “Let the swan fly away,”
And drove it into full view.
Unable to contain his excitement,
Semetey came riding up.
Then Kulchoro spoke these words,
Uttering an uncanny thought no man could know:
“Understand my precious words;
Blessed elder, heed what I say!
Let us not set the bird upon the swan,
And not drink our fill of joy.
I have looked upon this swan;
When it calls with that resonant cry,
Its voice is unlike a swan’s.
When it shakes itself like drifting sand,
Its form changes a thousand ways.
It must be one of the spirits,
The very embodiment of a sacred power.
It has transformed itself into a swan;
My poor elder, hear my words:
It is the source of some great calamity,
A swan come from Mecca,
And it has five young.
Let us not bring it down for nothing,
And fall into its curse.
Bloodthirsty elder, listen:
If we fly a bird at this swan of omen,
It will bring shame upon us.
This swan is no ordinary creature;
It has a form resembling a human,
Or else it may transform
And cast its demon upon us.
It is a swan of wondrous power,
One of the miracles!”
While the boy spoke in this way,
The tiger swelled with daring,
And with a booming voice
Spoke to Kulchoro:
“How much sin can there be in a swan?
Boy, you have grown quite mad.
For no good reason you hunger
To say, ‘I shall fly the bird.’
Though still a boy yourself,
You stand there like a bakshy,
Reciting every omen;
You have become a fine one indeed.
Taking omens from things that do not exist,
You have frightened yourself,
Muttering so many words
That you bar my way.
If it is a swan come from Mecca,
If it has five young,
Let it face me and swallow me;
If it is a swan of wondrous power,
Let it kill me outright.
Is there sin in taking a swan?
Can one prosper by fearing a bird?
Can the sin of killing a swan
Be greater than that of killing a man?
When I had reached the age of twelve,
There in the fortress of Bukhara,
When my father Temir Khan
Agreed to what I asked,
And held the funeral feast for my father Manas,
I began my feats of destruction:
I tore one arm completely
From the camel-strong wrestler.
Where then was my death?
Where did sin overtake me?
When I migrated to Talas,
I loaded my cartridge pouch and fired,
And among the Kokand champions,
Beginning with Janaaly and Karach,
I devoured them all without remainder.
Where then was my death?
Where did sin overtake me?”
